meta.title: Where does the internet live? · The cloud was never weightless

hero.title: Where does the internet live?
hero.sub: A 3-minute walk from your phone to the buildings behind it.

steps.title: You use it every day.
steps.lead: You tap. Your device turns that into information that can travel.
steps.note: Each tap becomes data: small packets of 1s and 0s.

steps.title: It travels through the air, through cables, through fibre.
steps.lead: Fibre: strands of glass that carry data as pulses of light.

steps.title: We call where it goes “the cloud.”
steps.lead: The cloud is a metaphor.
steps.note: It means computers you use over the internet, owned by someone else.

steps.title: This is where the cloud becomes physical.
steps.lead: The internet feels invisible. Its infrastructure isn't.

quote.text: “A model for enabling … on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources …”

steps.title: So, what's inside?
steps.lead: A building designed to keep computing equipment running.
steps.note: Four systems: compute, connect, power, cool.

steps.title: The machines.
steps.lead: Servers process, store and move information. They use about 60% of a data center's electricity, on average.
steps.note: A server is a computer with no screen, built to run all day for many users.
steps.hint: Tap a rack to open one server.

steps.title: The machines have to talk.
steps.lead: Information comes in. Information goes out.
steps.note: Switches pass data between servers; fibre links the building to the rest of the internet.

steps.title: The machines need power.
steps.lead: If the grid fails: UPS for seconds, generator for hours.
steps.note: UPS: batteries that take over instantly, until the diesel generators start.

steps.title: The machines produce heat.
steps.lead: Almost all the electricity a server uses ends up as heat. Cool air goes in; warm air is pulled out.

steps.title: Compute. Connect. Power. Cool.
steps.lead: Remove one, and the system changes.

steps.title: {time}. The building is operating.
steps.narration: It never sleeps. The clock changes. The infrastructure keeps working.
steps.lead: 06:00 · 12:00 · 18:00 · 24:00. The clock changes. The infrastructure keeps working.
steps.hint: Drag the dial to turn the clock.

steps.title: The power keeps flowing.
steps.lead: About 485 TWh worldwide in 2025. Projected: about 950 TWh by 2030, roughly double.

steps.title: Small globally. Concentrated locally.
steps.note: A small share of the world's electricity, but each building draws its share from one local grid connection.

steps.title: Electricity goes in. Heat has to come out.
steps.lead: Some of the heat leaves through water.
steps.note: Cooling towers shed heat by evaporating water. That water is used up, not returned.

steps.title: Google's data centers used about 29.5 billion litres of water in 2024.
steps.note: That is the total across its whole fleet, not one building.

steps.title: The digital world has a physical bill.
steps.lead: Energy · Water · Building · Materials
steps.note: Everything from the last two chapters, on one receipt. Tap a cost to open it.

steps.title: Materials: copper, cobalt, tantalum.
steps.lead: Can we trace a server back to a mine? Not automatically.
steps.note: Copper carries power and data. Cobalt goes into batteries. Tantalum goes into capacitors on circuit boards.

control.show: Look closer: where did this come from?

steps.title: A server has a footprint before it is switched on.
steps.note: Mining, manufacturing and shipping all use energy. This is called the embodied footprint.

steps.title: Now, here. How many data centers does Nepal have?
steps.lead: Take a guess.

control.after: There is no single answer. It depends on what you count.

steps.title: It depends on what you count.
steps.note: A company, a building and a backup site are all called a “data center”. Switch the rule and watch the number change.

steps.title: Most are in the Kathmandu Valley. Backups sit elsewhere.
steps.note: A disaster-recovery site keeps a copy of the data far away, in case the main building fails. Tap a marker for details.

steps.title: A new rule:
steps.lead: the Data Center and Cloud Service Directives, 2081.
steps.note: Providers must now register with the Department of Information Technology and meet security and privacy standards.

steps.title: It doesn't end when it leaves the rack.
steps.lead: Reuse · Refurbish · Recycle · Discard
steps.note: Servers are usually replaced after a few years. Tap a path to see what happens.

steps.title: 62 million tonnes of e-waste worldwide in 2022.
steps.lead: 22.3% formally recycled.
steps.note: “Formally recycled” means documented collection and recycling. The rest is not tracked.

steps.title: Nepal: about 41.5 million kg a year.
steps.lead: 1.4 kg per person.
steps.note: All e-waste, not data centers only.

steps.title: What should we ask about a data center?
steps.lead: Tap a card to read its questions. Then pick the one that matters most to you.

blocks.p: A transmitter switches a light on and off very fast. Each flash pattern stands for 1s and 0s.
The light stays inside the strand and travels to the far end, where a receiver reads the pulses back as data.

nist.title: Where does “the cloud” come from?

blocks.p: “Cloud computing is a model for enabling ubiquitous, convenient, on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources …”

nist.cite: Mell, P. & Grance, T. (2011). The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing. NIST.

compute.title: Compute

blocks.p: A computer built to run all day and answer requests from many people at once. A data center holds thousands of them in tall racks.
Mostly to cooling, plus storage, network equipment and power conversion.

terms.def: Uninterruptible power supply: a battery that keeps servers running during a power cut.
A diesel engine that provides power during longer outages.
Computer room air conditioning: cools the servers so they do not overheat.
How much data can move through a network connection at once.

compute.cite: International Energy Agency (2025). Energy and AI. IEA, Paris.

blocks.p: 1 TWh is 1 billion kilowatt-hours. About 485 TWh were used by data centers worldwide in 2025.
About 950 TWh by 2030, roughly double. This is a projection, not a measurement.
Cooling towers shed heat by evaporating water. That water is used up, not returned.
About 29.5 billion litres in 2024, across all of Google's data centers. It is a company total, not one building.
Carries power and data.
Goes into batteries.
Goes into capacitors on circuit boards.
A server passes through a mine, a material, a component and a factory. Each step is run by different companies, so the chain is not recorded automatically.
Mining, manufacturing and shipping all use energy. That footprint is counted before the server runs a single task.

ups.label: UPS (Battery Backup)
ups.desc: A battery backup that kicks in the instant power cuts out.

generator.desc: A backup generator that keeps the lights on during longer outages.

network_core.desc: Connects every server rack together at high speed.

pdu.desc: Sends power from the UPS to each server rack.

fire_suppression.desc: Puts out fires without damaging the equipment.
